title: Phase Kernel Lifts Capacity of Dense Associative Memory
claim: Linear kernels give narrow, confusable basins and retrieval failure; our nonlinear kernel shapes energy into broad basins and far higher capacity.
layout: 3 panels: parallel flowcharts, paired energy contour maps, bar charts; ✗/✓ marks
description: Three panels. (a) shows two parallel vertical flowcharts that start from a shared 'Stored Patterns' box. The left branch is gray (Linear Kernel → Narrow Basins → Mem Confusion → Retrieval Failure, marked with a red ✗). The right branch is blue (S-Hop Kernel → Broad Basins → Energy Shaping → Robust Retrieval, marked with a green ✓). (b) stacks two viridis-colored energy contour maps with streamlines and two starred memories m1 and m2. The MHN (linear) map has a singular point where its energy basins merge. The S-Hop (nonlinear) map has two distinct, smooth basins. (c) stacks two bar charts, for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, of critical capacity. A tall red S-Hop bar towers over tiny U-Hop, MHN and C-Hop bars, with '≥50×' arrows between them. The eye goes first to the color contrast in (a) and the tall red bars in (c).
caption: Framework, energy landscape, and capacity gains of S-Hop. (a) Schematic of the energyshaping motivation for stored patterns. (b) Illustrative 2D energy contours around m1, m2, independently scaled to [0, 1] for each kernel. (c) Retrieval-load summaries on CIFAR-10 (d = 3072) and ImageNet (224 × 224, d = 150528) for S-Hop, U-Hop [7], MHN [1], and Cosine Hopfield Network (C-Hop). S-Hop achieves passing-load ratios of over 50× than the previous methods.
abstract: Dense associative memory underlies modern attention mechanisms; however, Modern Hopfield Networks (MHNs) with linear kernels yield overlapping attractor basins and spurious states under high memory load, limiting their theoretically exponential storage capacity in practice. We construct a class of nonlinear phase kernels that modify the energy landscape and retrieval dynamics, and prove that these kernels preserve exponential storage capacity and local fixed-point convergence under given conditions on kernel smoothness, memory separation, and memory distributions. The framework is instantiated by the Sigmoidal Phase Hopfield Network (S-Hop), which guarantees monotone energy descent and mitigates practical capacity loss. S-Hop has $8.3\times$ and $4\times$ gains in one-step noisy retrieval load over Uniform Hopfield Networks (U-Hop) on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet respectively, and reaches a $50\times$ gain in first-failure load for ImageNet. The results demonstrate that phase kernels provide a principled route to robust dense associative memory.
